stem_md:
Let  $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$  be an infinite sequence of positive integers, and let  $N$  be a positive integer. Suppose that, for each  $n > N$ ,  $a_n$  is equal to the number of times  $a_{n-1}$  appears in the list  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n-1}$ .

Prove that at least one of the sequence  $a_1, a_3, a_5, \dots$  and  $a_2, a_4, a_6, \dots$  is eventually periodic.

(An infinite sequence  $b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots$  is eventually periodic if there exist positive integers  $p$  and  $M$  such that  $b_{m+p} = b_m$  for all  $m \ge M$ .)
solution_md:
Interesting combinatorics in disguise of sequence. The key is to prove that sufficiently large numbers appear finitely many times in such sequence, and such number of appearance should be equal for all sufficiently large numbers.

Denote  $f(n, i)$  the number of occurrences of  $i$  among the first  $n$  entries  $a_1, \ldots, a_n$  of the sequence. We have  $a_n = f(n-1, a_{n-1})$  for all  $n > N$ . Select a sufficiently large integer  $M > N$  such that  $f(N, j) = 0$  for all  $j \ge M$  and  $f(N, j) < M$  for all  $j <M$ . 

We begin by observing that starting from  $n = N+1$ , any pairs  $(a_n, a_{n+1})$  will appear only once in the sequence. It means that all the numbers that precedents a same number  $j$  in the sequence must be mutually different. **Claim 1:** For all  $t > N$  and  $M \le i < j$ ,  $f(t, i) \ge f(t, j)$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>WLOG assume that  $j = i+1$ . For any  $t > N$ , note that since  $f(N, j) = f(N, i) = 0$ , all occurrences of  $i$  and  $j$  must be in  $a_{N+1}, \ldots, a_t$ . Let  $i_1, \ldots, i_{f(t, j)}$  be the indices such that  $a_{i_l} = j$  for  $1\le l \le f(t, j)$ , then we have  $f(i_l - 1, a_{i_l - 1}) = j$ . There must then exist  $k_l < i_l-1$  such that  $f(k_l, a_{i_l - 1}) = i$  and  $a_{k_l} = a_{i_l-1}$  , and thus  $a_{k_l+1} = i$ . Note that all  $a_{i_l-1}$  should be mutually different, so all  $k_l$  are mutually different. So  $i$  occurs at least as many times as  $j$  within  $a_1, \ldots, a_t$ . This implies  $f(t, i) \ge f(t, j)$ .</details>**Claim 2:**  $f(t, K)\le K-1$  for all  $t$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Assume the contradiction and consider the indice  $t$  such that  $a_t = K$  and  $f(t, K) = K$ . Let  $i_1<i_2<\ldots <i_K$  be the indices such that  $a_{i_l} = K$ . Note that all  $a_{i_l-1}$  must be mutually different, so one of  $a_{i_l-1}$  is greater than  $K$ . Then,  $f(i_l-1, a_{i_l-1}) = K > f(t-1, K) \ge f(i_l-1, K)$ , contradicts claim 1.</details>

Due to claim 1 and claim 2, for all  $t$  and  $i \ge K$ , we have  $f(t, i) \le K-1$ . This means that for any given  $i$ ,  $\lim_{t\to \infty} f(t, i)$  converges to  $B_i$  for some  $B_i \le K-1$  (due to monotonicity in  $t$ ). Due to claim 1 again we can see that  $B_i\ge B_j$  for all  $K\le i < j$ , so  $\lim_{i\to \infty} B_i = c$  for some  $0\le c \le K-1$ . Hence, there exists constants  $T, M, c$  such that  $f(t, i) = c$  for all  $t > T, i > M$ . **Claim 3:**  $c \ge 1$  and the numbers  $1, 2, \ldots, c$  are the only numbers that occur infinitely often in the sequence.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>To show that  $c \ge 1$  it is sufficient to show that any number  $x$  must occur once in the sequence  $(a_n)$ . Note that there must exist a number  $a$  that occurs infinitely many times in the sequence. Let  $l$  be the indices of its  $x^\text{th}$  occurrence, then  $a_{l+1} = x$ , as desired.

Now it is obvious to see that  $1, 2, \ldots, c$  occur infinitely often in the sequence. We show that any  $i > c$  does not occur infinitely often. Assume the contradiction, then since for all  $j > M$ ,  $f(t, j)$  is eventually  $c$ , or  $f(t, j)$  will occur only  $c$  times in the sequence, then after the occurrence of  $j$  it can only be the numbers from  $1, 2, \ldots, c$ . This means that the occurrence of  $i > c$  can only be after a number  $j' < M$ . Since there are only finitely many such  $j'$ , the occurrence of  $i$  must be finite.</details>

Claim 3 implies that there exists sufficiently large integers  $N'$  and  $M$  such that for all  $n > N'$ , it is either that  $a_n > M$ , or  $a_n \le c$ . Note that we can again select  $N'$  to be large enough so that  $f(N', i) > c$  for all  $1\le i \le c$ , so that any numbers that comes after  $1\le i \le c$  must be larger than  $M$ . This creates an alternating sequence between "large" and "small" number. It is sufficient to show that the sequence of "small" number is eventually periodic. The tricky part of this is to control the gap between occurrences of the same number. **Claim 4:** There exists a constant  $D$  such that for any  $t$ ,  $\max_{1\le i \le c} f(t, i) - \min_{1\le i\le c} f(t, i) \le D$ . 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>For any  $1\le x < y\le c$ , there is a constant  $L_{x, y}$  for any  $t$ ,  $f(t, x) \ge f(t, y) - L_{x, y}$ . Note that when  $t > N'$ , any occurrences of  $y$  must be precedented by an occurrence of a number  $j > M$ . Such  $j > M$  must give an occurrence of  $x < y$  some time before that. 

Let  $L = \max(L_{x, y})$  over all  $x < y$ . Then, if we assume the contradiction that  $\max_{1\le i \le c} f(t, i) - \min_{1\le i\le c} f(t, i)$  is not uniformly bounded on  $t$ , then there must be a sufficiently large  $t$  and an  $1\le i \le c-1$  such that  $\min_{1\le j \le i} f(t, j) > \max_{i+1\le j \le c} f(t, j)$ . In fact, let  $t$  be the number such that  $\max_{1\le i \le c} f(t, i) - \min_{1\le i\le c} f(t, i) > 3L$ . Let  $j_1, j_2$  be the indices that  $f(t, j_1) = \max_{1\le i\le c} f(t, i), f(t, j_2) = \min_{1\le i\le c} f(t, i)$ . By claim 3, we must have  $j_1 < j_2$ . Furthermore,  $f(t, i) \ge f(t, j_1) - L$  for all  $i < j_1$ , and  $f(t_i) \le f(t, j_2) + L$  for all  $i > j_2$ . Since there can't be  $j_1 < k_1 < k_2 < j_2$  such that  $f(t, k_2) \ge f(t, j_1) - L$  and  $f(t, k_1) \le f(t, j_2) + L$ , it must be the case that there is an index  $k$  such that  $f(t, i) \ge f(t, j_1) - L)$  for all  $i \le k$ , and  $f(t, i) \le f(t, j_2) + L$  for all  $i > k$ . Since  $f(t, j_1) - L > f(t, j_2) + L$ , we arrive at the claim.

Then, at the first time  $t$  that this happens,  $a_t \le i$ , and  $a_{t+1}$  is larger than  $\max_{i+1\le j \le c} f(t, j)$ . Then,  $a_{t+2}$  must be in  $1, 2, \ldots, i$ , and we can use induction to show that from then on, no more occurrences of  $i+1, \ldots, c$  can happen, which contradicts claim 3.</details>

For a number  $n > M$ , define  $i_{n, 1} < i_{n, 2} < \ldots < i_{n, c}$  the indices that  $a_{i_{n, k}} = n$ . Denote the difference tuple  $T_n = (i_{n, 2} - i_{n, 1}, \ldots, i_{n, c} - i_{n, c-1})$ . **Claim 5:** There is a constant  $D'$  such that  $i_{n, h} - i_{n, h-1} \le D'$  for all  $n > M$  and  $2\le h\le c$ . 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Note that the difference between  $f(t, i)$  and  $f(t, j)$  for  $1\le i < j\le c$  is bounded above by  $D$  at any time  $t$  (claim 4). Consider  $a_{i_{n, h-1}} = n, a_{i_{n, h-1}+1} = h-1$  and  $a_{i_{n, h}} = n, a_{i_{n, h}+1} = h$ . Note that for  $i_{n, h-1} \le t \le i_{n, h}-2$ , among  $f(t, 1), \ldots, f(t, c)$ , there are exactly  $h-1$  values that are at least  $n$ , and all other values must be smaller than  $n$ . As the gap between the maximum and minimum of  $f(t, i)$  is at most  $D$ , we can see that the values initially smaller than  $n$  must be at least  $n-D$ , and thus the appearance of  $a$  such that  $f(i_{n, h-1}, a) < n$  between  $i_{n, h-1} \le t \le i_{n, h}-2$  can only be at most  $D$ . Likewise, the appearance of  $a$  such that  $f(i_{n, h-1}, a) \ge n$  between  $i_{n, h-1} \le t \le i_{n, h}-2$  is also at most  $D$ , as  $f(t, a)$  can only increase at maximal to  $n+D$ .

This implies a rough bound  $i_{n, h} - i_{n, h-1} \le 2Dc$ . Let  $D' = 2Dc$  and we are done.</details>

Now, since there are at most  $D'^{c-1}$  values for the tuples  $T_n$  for  $n \ge M$ ,  $T_n$  must be eventually periodic. Let  $T$  be the period of  $T_n$ , and let  $b = i_{n+T, 1} - i_{n, 1}$ , then for every sufficiently large  $n$  and  $1\le h\le c$ , we have  $i_{n+T, h} - i_{n, h} = i_{n+T, H} - i_{n+T, 1} - (i_{n, h} - i_{n, 1}) + i_{n+T,1} - i_{n, 1} = i_{n+T,1} - i_{n, 1}$ . Now, we can proceed similar to claim 5 to show that there is a constant  $B$  such that  $i_{n+T,1} - i_{n, 1} \le B$  for all  $n$  (brief idea: the difference  $i_{n+T,1} - i_{n, 1}$  is the difference between the  $n^\text{th}$  1 and  $(n+T)^\text{th}$  1, hence occurrences of  $2, \ldots, c$  can only be at most  $T+2D$  for each of them). This again means that  $i_{n+T,1} - i_{n, 1} \le B$  is eventually periodic, so there is a period  $C$  such that  $i_{n+T+C,1} - i_{n+C, 1} = i_{n+T,1} - i_{n, 1}$  for all  $n$  sufficiently large. 

*It is important to note that eventual periodicity is implied due to a non trivial fact that once a pattern repeats, then by induction it will keep repeating. I'll leave this as some details for others to work on.*

Let  $b = i_{n+T+C, 1} - i_{n, 1}$ . Then for any  $n$  sufficiently large and  $1\le h\le c, a_{i_{n, h} +1} = h = a_{i_{n+T+C, h} + 1} = a_{i_{n, h} + b+1}$ . This implies that the "small" sequence is eventually periodic, as desired.

Due to my laziness, I might have avoided many small details of the proof. Any comments are appreciated.

A couple others have already mentioned this is not true, but here is an argument that kills this statement and many others. The point is that given any infinite sequence of the type given in the problem, we can stop the sequence at any point, adjust the value of $N$ to be a few entries further than where we currently are, and add any small entries we would like without influencing the later portion of the sequence. For example, given the sequence: \begin{align*} 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 1, 6, \ldots \end{align*} I can adjust the value of $N$ up to $8$ and start the sequence as follows: \begin{align*} \textcolor{red}{1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4,} 1, 5, 1, 6, \ldots \end{align*} This tells us that unless we modify what starting sequences we can have, there's no guarantee that we can make the ``corner square'' nice in any way. So once you get that you are alternating between big and small numbers you know that really you have to work with the dynamics of what kinds of subsequences the small squares can form.

In this problem, there were  $88$  contestants who made partial progress,  $12$  who nearly solved it, and  $8$  who solved it entirely. I didn't feel there was a breakthrough point in this problem, but I found it very challenging, nevertheless.

Instead of going back along the sequence whenever generating a successive term, I marked every new term with a dot in a row of its number, left aligned. For example, if  $a_N$  occurs  $n$  times, then I put a dot in row  $n$ . Then, if there are  $n'$  dots in this row, I put a dot in row  $n'$  after that, iterating the rule. Using this notation, it is easy to test many examples.

Let's draw an  $L\times L$  black box around all the dots counting the multiplicities before the rule begins to apply. Upon iteration, I claim there will be three kinds of dots: inside the box, in the first  $L$  rows outside it ( $\rightarrow$ ), or in the first  $L$  columns outside it ( $\downarrow$ ). After a dot in the first  $L$  columns, there will be a dot in row number at most  $L$ . If such a dot is outside the box, the dot after that has row number more than  $L$ , but no more than  $L$  dots can be in that row already, because those count how many dots occur in a row numbered at most  $L$ . Thus, by induction, these are the three kinds of dots, and only finitely many occur inside the box. Moreover, once those have been exhausted,  $\rightarrow$  and  $\downarrow$  dots alternate. In all examples I have checked, in this regime, the  $\rightarrow$  sequence is periodic, but I did not have to prove this conjectural fact.

Returning to the  $\rightarrow$  dots, which all arise according to the rule, the  $\downarrow$  dots, which arise from the  $\rightarrow$  dots, number as many in each row as there are  $\rightarrow$  dots there are in the respective column. If a  $\rightarrow$  dot arises following a  $\downarrow$  dot, its row number is equal to this. Hence, the configuration of  $\rightarrow$  dots and current row value determine the next value if the  $\rightarrow$  and  $\downarrow$  dots arise alternately. In particular, the next row value is given by the number of dots in the current column.

For the conclusion, suppose the value  $n$  appears in the sequence. That means there were  $n$  occurrences of the previous term, and so there were  $n-1$  occurrences of it beforehand. By definition,  $n-1$  appeared thereafter, excepting at most  $L$  cases. Thus, we obtain an injective map from times that  $n$  appears to times that  $n-1$  appears or  $L$  exceptions. Furthermore, if the value that occurs  $n-1$  times will occur  $n$  times, too, then this map has an inverse. If  $n$  appears infinitely many times, then every value larger than  $L$  occurs  $n$  times, and so this holds with at most  $L$  exceptions.

Let  $m\le L$  be the largest value that appears infinitely many times. It follows inductively that  $m-1,m-2,\dots,1$  also appear infinitely many times. Now it is clear that between these rows, the number of dots differ by a bounded amount, and it is these differences, along with a current value, that can determine the next value with differences. By quoting how a sequence with finite range in which every term is determined by the preceding one shall be periodic eventually, it follows that every other term, the row values of the  $\rightarrow$  dots, yields an eventually periodic sequence.

I don't think there is a single idea that solves this problem. Most of the contestants in our team made all the necessary observations. Unfortunately, without rigorous proofs. So, the difficulty of this problem lies in the technique of proving the facts we know. The main observation is that the sequence eventually alternates between *small-large-small*, ... numbers, where the "small" numbers are picked from the set  $\{1,2,\dots,\ell\}$ , for some  $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$  . The large number that follows each small number equals its frequency in the sequence up to the moment. Proving this gets you 3 points. The additional 4 points are for proving that the pattern of the small numbers becomes periodic at some point. The last sentence is the most difficult to prove. It's helpful to interpret the sequence in the following way.    

Imagine finite number of checkers enumerated from  $1$  to  $\ell$ , placed on some natural numbers on  $Ox$  axis. The checkers are the "small" numbers and the  $i$ -th checker is places on the number equal to the number of occurrences of the small number  $i$  in the sequence  $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{T}$  up to the moment  $T$ . At each subsequent moment one of the checkers, say the  $j$ -th, moves from position  $b_j$  to position  $b_j+1$ , which means that the number of occurrences of  $j$  increases from  $b_j$  to  $b_{j}+1$ . That is, when a checker  $j$  steps on a position  $b:=b_j+1$ , two new numbers are placed at the end of the sequence:  $j$  and  $b$ . We want to translate the rule of how the sequence evolves to meet this interpretation. So, after the checker  $j$  steps on  $b$ -th position, what is the next checker to be moved forward? The answer is: the checker whose number is equal to the number of occurrences of  $b$  in the original sequence so far. But  $b$  appears in the sequence if and only if a checker steps on the  $b$ -th position. This means that after checker  $j$  moves to the  $b$ -th position, then the next checker to move will be one whose number is equal to the number of checkers that have already stepped on the  $b$ -th position, that is, the number of checkers currently at positions  $b, b+1,\dots.$ This interpretation makes it easier to prove that the ensemble of checkers moves in a pack, i.e. no one is left behind. Once this is proven, the rest is easy. The patterns of the moving checkers are finitely many and two positions will repeat. Since each subsequent move is determined by this pattern, the moves from here on out will follow a periodical cycle.

**Solution.** As above we use a grid to visualize the problem. Consider points in  $\mathbb{N}^2$  where  $(x,y)$  corresponds to the value  $x$  appearing in the sequence for the  $y$ -th time. For  $n>N$  we have that the point corresponding to  $a_n$  is  $(a_n,a_{n+1})$ . To get to our next point we can imagine reflecting our current point over the line  $y=x$  and then moving to the first available spot in the column.

Suppose all points in the start ( $n\leq N$ ) are contained in  $[1,M]\times[1,M]$ . We claim that all points in the sequence will either have  $x\leq M$  or  $y\leq M$ . Consider the first point  $P=(p,q)$  that violates this. Then we must have  $q=M+1$  and  $p>M$ . But all points on the line with  $x=q$  must have had their predecessor lie on the line  $y=q$ . But there are only  $M$  points in the region with  $y=q$  so this is impossible.

Since numbers at most  $M$  are the only candidates for numbers that appear infinitely often let  $m$  be the largest such number that appears infinitely often. At any point after  $[1,M]\times[1,M]$  is filled in let  $y_1,y_2,\dots,y_m$  denote the highest  $y$ -coordinate over the lines  $x=1,2,\dots,m$ . We claim that all differences  $y_i-y_j$  are bounded in both directions. Say  $i<j$ . Then  $y_i-y_j$  is bounded below as any number must appear  $i$  times before it appears  $j$  times except for the first  $N$  numbers. Now suppose there exists an  $L$  such that   $$ y_1,y_2,\dots,y_i>L>y_{i+1},\dots,y_m. $$   We show this is not possible. Consider the most recent point placed with  $y\leq i$ . Notice for  $t>M$  points on the line  $x=t$  correspond to points on the line  $y=t$ . Thus after this happens we will only stay in the region  $y\leq L$  or  $x\leq L$ . This however contradicts the minimality of  $m$ .

Combined with the fact that for  $i<j$  we have  $y_i-y_j$  is bounded below we get that the the range of the sequence  $y_i$  is bounded. Similarly we have that the range of  $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_m$  is bounded. However notice that we now only have a finite number of states. Since we move according to an algorithm, eventually the sequence  $y_2-y_1,\dots,y_m-y_1$  will be periodic. Notice that every other term one of the  $y_i$  will increase by  $1$  and that term will be equal to  $i$ . Hence on these terms the sequence will be periodic, as desired.

This is very obvious. Then, the number of Hiura numbers is finite, and if  $k$  is the largest Hiura number, then  $1, 2, \dots, k$  are Hiura numbers (call the set of all Hiura numbers be  $H$ ), and  $k+1, k+2, \dots$  are non-Hiura numbers. Then we get the fact that there are only finite numbers whose time of appearance exceeds the largest Hiura number.   $\textbf{Claim 3.}$  Exactly one of two sequences  $\{a_{2n}\}$ ,  $\{a_{2n+1}\}$  is bounded.   $\textbf{Proof.}$  Let  $M$  be sufficiently large. \]

E = \{r \in H \mid r \text{ appears at least } a_{2n-1} \text{ times from } a_1 \text{ to } a_{2n-1}\}
\]  
\[

Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with  $AB < AC < BC$ . Let the incenter and incircle of triangle  $ABC$  be  $I$  and  $\omega$ , respectively. Let  $X$  be the point on line  $BC$  different from  $C$  such that the line through  $X$  parallel to  $AC$  is tangent to  $\omega$ . Similarly, let  $Y$  be the point on line  $BC$  different from  $B$  such that the line through  $Y$  parallel to  $AB$  is tangent to  $\omega$ . Let  $AI$  intersect the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  at  $P \ne A$ . Let  $K$  and  $L$  be the midpoints of  $AC$  and  $AB$ , respectively. 
Prove that  $\angle KIL + \angle YPX = 180^{\circ}$ .

*Proposed by Dominik Burek, Poland*

stem_md:
Let  $\mathbb{Q}$  be the set of rational numbers. A function  $f: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$  is called aquaesulian if the following property holds: for every  $x,y \in \mathbb{Q}$ ,
\[ f(x+f(y)) = f(x) + y \quad \text{or} \quad f(f(x)+y) = x + f(y). \]
Show that there exists an integer  $c$  such that for any aquaesulian function  $f$  there are at most  $c$  different rational numbers of the form  $f(r) + f(-r)$  for some rational number  $r$ , and find the smallest possible value of  $c$ .
solution_md:
SolutionThe answer is $c=\boxed{2}$ , achieved by $f(x) = 2\lfloor x\rfloor - x$ . This works because if $\{x\} \leq \{y\}$ , then \begin{align*} f(f(x)+y) &= f(2\lfloor x\rfloor + y-x) &= 2\lfloor 2\lfloor x\rfloor + y-x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor -y+x &= 2\lfloor x\rfloor + 2\lfloor y-x\rfloor + x-y, \end{align*} and $$ f(y)+x = 2\lfloor y\rfloor + x-y, $$ and so their difference is $$ 2\lfloor x\rfloor + 2\lfloor y-x\rfloor - 2\lfloor y\rfloor = -2[\{x\} + \{y-x\} - \{y\}] = 0, $$ since $\{x\} \leq \{y\}$ . If $\{y\} \leq \{x\}$ , then $f(f(y)+x) = f(x)+y$ instead by our above work. If $x\in \mathbb{Z}$ , $$ f(x)+f(-x) = (2\lfloor x\rfloor - x) + (2\lfloor -x\rfloor - (-x)) = x+(-x) = 0, $$ and if $x\in \mathbb{Q}\setminus \mathbb{Z}$ , $$ f(x)+f(-x) = (2\lfloor x\rfloor -x) + (2\lfloor -x\rfloor - (-x)) = 2(\lfloor x\rfloor + \lfloor -x\rfloor) = -2, $$ so there are indeed exactly two possible values of $f(x)+f(-x)$ as $x$ ranges over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Now, we show that we must have $c\leq 2$ . Let $P(x, y)$ denote the assertion, as usual.**Claim: ** $f(0)=0$ and $f$ is injective at $0$ .**Proof: ** First, we will show that $0\in \text{Im }f$ . To show this, we assume the contrary. Then, $$ P(x, -f(x))\implies f(0) = x + f(-f(x)) \text{ or } f(f(-f(x)) + x) = 0. $$ Because of our assumption of the contrary, we cannot have the second option as it would imply that $0\in \text{Im }f$ . Thus, we must have the first option, i.e. $f(0)= x+f(-f(x))$ . But, now set $x = f(0)$ to get $f(-f(f(0))) = 0$ , so $0\in \text{Im }f$ , a contradiction. Thus, we have a contradiction and so we must have $0\in \text{Im }f$ . Now, suppose that $f(r) = 0$ for some $r\in \mathbb{Q}$ . Then, $$ P(r, r)\implies f(f(r)+r) = f(r)+r, $$ but since $f(r)=0$ , this means $f(r) = r$ , but then $r=0$ . Thus, it follows that $f(0)=0$ and $f$ is injective at $0$ , as desired. $\square$ Now, look at the assertion $P(x, -f(x))$ again. It implies that $$ f(-f(x)) = -x \text{ or } f(f(-f(x)) + x) = 0. $$ Note that since $f$ is injective at $0$ , the second option is equivalent to $f(-f(x)) + x = 0$ , i.e. $f(-f(x)) = -x$ , which is equivalent to the first option. Thus, we must have that $$ f(-f(x)) = -x $$ for all $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ . Now, note that this implies injectivity, since if $f(a) = f(b)$ for some $a, b\in \mathbb{Q}$ , then $$ -a = f(-f(a)) = f(-f(b)) = -b, $$ so $a=b$ . Now, let $S = \{x \mid f(x) = x\}$ . Note that $0\in S$ .**Claim: ** If $s, t\in S$ , then $s+t\in S$ . Furthermore, $-s\in S$ .**Proof: ** For the first part, note that $$ P(s, t)\implies f(s+t) = s+t. $$ Now, by our newfound property ( $f(-f(x)) = -x$ ), we have that by setting $x = s$ , we have that $f(-s) = -s$ , as desired. $\square$ Now, if $S = \{0\}$ , then since $P(x, x)\implies f(x+f(x)) = x+f(x)$ , then we have that $x+f(x) = 0$ for all $x$ , i.e. $f(x) = -x$ , so $f(x)+f(-x) = 0$ always, and so there is $1\leq 2$ possible value of $f(x)+f(-x)$ . Otherwise, assume that $S\neq \{0\}$ . Then, there exists an element $K$ of $S$ not equal to $0$ . Then, by the above claim, it is clear that for any integer $n$ , $nK\in S$ . Now, note that by our newfound property ( $f(-f(x)) = -x$ ), we have that \begin{align*} P(x, y) &\implies f(f(x)+y) = x+f(y) \text{ or } f(x+f(y)) = f(x) + y &\implies f(f(x)+y) = x+f(y) \text{ or } f(-f(x+f(y))) = f(-f(x)-y) &\implies f(f(x)+y) = x + f(y) \text{ or } -x-f(y) = f(-f(x)-y) &\implies f(f(x)+y) = x+f(y) \text{ or } f(-f(x)-y) = -x-f(y). \end{align*} Thus, \begin{align*} P(-f(x), y) &\implies f(f(-f(x)) + y) = -f(x) + f(y) \text{ or } f(-f(-f(x)) - y) = f(x) - f(y) &\implies f(-x+y) = -f(x) + f(y) \text{ or }f(x-y) = f(x) - f(y) &\implies f(x)-f(y) \in \{f(x-y), -f(-x+y)\}. \end{align*} Let the assertion to this be $Q(x, y)$ . Now, fix some $r\in \mathbb{Q}$ .**Claim: ** For all integers $n$ , $f(nr) + f(-nr) \in \{f(r) + f(-r), 0\}$ .**Proof: ** First of all, if we have that $f(r) + f(-r) = 0$ , then $$ Q(x+r, x)\implies f(x+r) - f(x) \in \{f(r), -f(-r)\} = \{f(r)\}, $$ so $f(x+r) = f(x)+f(r)$ for all $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ , so $f(nr) = nf(r)$ for all $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ , and so $f(nr) + f(-nr) = 0$ . So, assume that $f(r) + f(-r) \neq 0$ . Let $a = f(r)$ and $b = f(-r)$ . Then, $$ Q(x+r,x)\implies f(x+r) - f(x) \in \{f(r), -f(-r)\} = \{a, -b\}, $$ so for all integers $n$ , $$ f(r(n+1)) - f(rn) \in \{a, -b\}. $$ Now, we show the claimed statement by induction on $n$ (it suffices to show it for $n\geq 1$ , as for $n=0$ it is clear since $f(0)=0$ , and $f(-nr)+f(-(-nr)) = f(nr) + f(-nr)$ ). Our base case $n=1$ is trivially true. Now, assume that for some $k\geq 1$ , we had that $f(kr) + f(-kr) \in \{a+b, 0\}$ . If $f(kr) + f(-kr) = a+b$ , then letting $x = f(kr)$ , we have $f(-kr) = a+b-x$ , so $$ f((k+1)r) \in \{x+a, x-b\}, $$ and $$ f((-k-1)r) \in \{(a+b-x)-a, (a+b-x)+b\} = \{b-x, a+2b-x\}. $$ Now, the only case for which $f((k+1)r) + f(-(k+1)r) \notin \{0, a+b\}$ is when $f((k+1)r) = x+a$ and $f((-k-1)r) = a+2b-x$ . However, note that $$ Q(kr, -r) \implies x-b = f(kr) - f(-r) \in \{f((k+1)r), -f((-k-1)r)\} = \{x+a, x-a-2b\}, $$ however $x-b = x+a$ implies that $a+b=0$ , but we are assuming $a+b\neq 0$ , and $x-b = x-a-2b$ implies that $a+b = 0$ as well, but we are assuming $a+b\neq 0$ . So, we have a contradiction, and so in all cases, we have that $f((k+1)r) + f((-k-1)r) \in \{0, a+b\}$ , so the inductive step is complete in the case that $f(kr) + f(-kr) = a+b$ . If $f(kr) + f(-kr) = 0$ , then letting $x = f(kr)$ , we have that $f(-kr) = -x$ . Then, $$ f((k+1)r)\in \{x+a, x-b\}, $$ and $$ f((-k-1)r)\in \{-x-a, -x+b\}. $$ The only case where $f((k+1)r) + f((-k-1)r) \notin \{0, a+b\}$ is when $f((k+1)r) = x-b$ and $f((-k-1)r) = -x-a$ . Assume for the sake of contradiction that we had this case. Then, I claim that $f((k+\ell)r) = x-b\ell$ and $f((-k-\ell)r) = -x-a\ell$ for all positive integers $\ell$ , and we will prove this by induction on $\ell$ , with our base case $\ell = 1$ already established. Assume that for some $\ell \geq 1$ , we had that $$ f((k+\ell)r) = x-b\ell $$ and $$ f((-k-\ell)r) = -x-a\ell. $$ Then, we have that $$ f((k+\ell+1)r)\in \{x-b\ell+a, x-b(\ell+1)\} $$ and $$ f((-k-\ell-1)r) \in \{-x-a(\ell+1), -x-a\ell+b\}. $$ Note that $$ Q((k+\ell)r, -r)\implies x-b(\ell+1) = f((k+\ell)r) - f(-r) \in \{f((k+\ell+1)r), -f((-k-\ell-1)r)\}, $$ so it follows that $f((k+\ell+1)r) = x-b(\ell+1)$ , since the other cases fail as $-b(\ell+1), -b\ell+a, a(\ell+1), a\ell-b$ are all distinct because $a+b\neq 0$ . Similarly, $$ Q(r, (-k-\ell)r) \implies x + a(\ell+1) = f(r) - f((-k-\ell)r) \in \{f((k+\ell+1)r, -f((-k-\ell-1)r)\}, $$ which implies that $f((-k-\ell-1)r) = -x-a(\ell+1)$ since the other options fail for the same reason as above. Thus, the induction (for the sub-claim) is proven and so $f((k+\ell)r) = x-b\ell$ and $f((-k-\ell)r) = -x-a\ell$ for all positive integers $\ell$ . Thus, for all integers $n\geq k+1$ , we have that $$ f(nr) + f(-nr) = -(a+b)(n-k) \neq 0. $$ However, note that there exists integers $n_1 \geq k+1$ and $n_2$ such that $n_1 r = n_2 K$ (here, $K$ was defined earlier to be a nonzero element of $S$ ). Then, since $K\in S$ , $n_2 K\in S$ , so $n_1 r\in S$ . Thus, $f(n_1r) = n_1r$ . Note that $-n_1 r = -n_2 K$ , so $-n_2 K\in S$ , and so $-n_1r\in S$ as well, so $f(-n_1r) = -n_1r$ . However, this means that $$ f(n_1r) + f(-n_1r) = 0, $$ a contradiction since $n_1 \geq k+1$ . Thus, our original assumption as false and so the only valid cases for $f((k+1)r)$ and $f((-k-1)r)$ are the ones summing to $0$ or $a+b$ , as desired. Thus, in all cases, the induction is complete, and so the claim is proven. $\square$ Now, to finish, assume for the sake of contradiction that there existed two distinct nonzero rationals $s$ and $t$ that can be expressed in the form $f(r) + f(-r)$ for some rational $r$ . Let $$ f(r_1) + f(-r_1) = s $$ and $$ f(r_2) + f(-r_2) = t $$ for rationals $r_1$ and $r_2$ . Note that $r_1, r_2 \neq 0$ since $s, t \neq 0$ . Then, note that there exists a rational $r_3$ such that $r_1 = r_3 m_1$ and $r_2 = r_3 m_2$ for integers $m_1$ and $m_2$ (such an $r_3$ exists since if $r_1 = \frac{p}{q}, r_2 = \frac{r}{s}$ , then say $r_3 = \frac{1}{qs}$ works). Then, we have that by the claim, $$ s, t = f(r_1)+f(-r_1), f(r_2) + f(-r_2) \in \{f(r_3) + f(-r_3), 0\}, $$ but both are nonzero, so they must both be equal to $f(r_3) + f(-r_3)$ . But since $s\neq t$ , this is a contradiction. Thus, we have a contradiction and so there are is at most $1$ nonzero rational that can be expressed in the form $f(r) + f(-r)$ for some rational $r$ . Thus, there are at most $2$ rationals that can be expressed in this form, as desired. $\blacksquare$
Remark on ConstructionI actually found this through erronous calculations (I somehow overlooked $s\in S\implies s/2 \in S$ ), persuading me to believe that if $S = \{x \mid f(x) = x\}$ and $T = \{x\mid f(x) = -x\}$ , then every $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ can be uniquely expressed as $s+t$ for some $s\in S$ and $t\in T$ . However, this lead me to discover a general family of solutions: Take some $S, T$ such that all $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ can be uniquely expressed as $s+t$ for some $s\in S$ and $t\in T$ . Further, suppose that if $x, y\in S$ , then $x+y\in S$ , and if $x, y\in T$ , at least one of $x-y, y-x$ is in $T$ . Then, the function $f$ taking $s+t$ to $s-t$ for all $s\in S$ , $t\in T$ works. This is because if $x, y\in \mathbb{Q}$ can be expressed as $s_1+t_1$ and $s_2+t_2$ , respectively, then $$ f(x)+y = f(s_1+t_1) + s_2 + t_2 = (s_1 + s_2) + (t_2-t_1) $$ and $$ f(y) + x = f(s_2+t_2) + s_1 + t_1 = (s_1+s_2) + (t_1-t_2), $$ and at least one of $t_1-t_2, t_2-t_1\in T$ , so if we WLOG suppose $t_1-t_2\in T$ , then since $s_1+s_2\in S$ , $(s_1+s_2) + (t_1-t_2)$ is the unique representation of $f(y)+x$ , so $$ f(f(y)+x) = f((s_1+s_2) + (t_1-t_2)) = (s_1+s_2) + (t_2-t_1) = f(x)+y. $$ I then took $S = \mathbb{Z}$ and $T = [0, 1)$ and then this led to $f(x) = f(\lfloor x\rfloor + \{x\}) = \lfloor x\rfloor - \{x\} = 2\lfloor x\rfloor - x$ .

This is such a beautiful problem, definitely my favorite one this year, by far.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>$c=2$ .</details>

<details><summary>Construction</summary>Take  $f(x)=[x]-\{x\}$ . First notice that  $f(x)+f(-x)=0$  if  $x\in\mathbb{Z}$  and  $-1$  if  $x\not\in\mathbb{Z}$ .
Now for every  $x,y\in \mathbb{R}$ , WLOG assume that  $\{x\}\geq \{y\}$ .
Then  $x+f(y) = [x]+[y]+\{x\}-\{y\}$  and  $y+f(x) = [x]+[y]+\{y\}-\{x\}$ .
Therefore  $f(x+f(y)) = y+f(x)$ , as desired.
This shows that  $c\geq 2$ .</details>

<details><summary>Proof that c cannot be larger</summary><u>Prop 1.</u>   $x+f(x)$  is a fixed point.
To see this, simply take  $x=y$  and see that in either case,  $f(x+f(x)) = x+f(x)$ .

<u>Prop 2.</u>  $f(0)=0$ .
<details><summary>Proof of Prop 2.</summary>Let  $S$  be the set of  $x$  such that  $f(x)=f(0)$ . Notice that  $0,f(0)\in S$  trivially and by Prop 1.
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that  $f(0)\neq 0$ .
Now if  $a\in S\backslash {0}$ , then by  $P(a,0)$  we see that either  $f(a+f(0))=f(a)$  or  $f(f(a))=a+f(0)$ .
The latter is clearly a contradiction as  $f(f(a)) = f(f(0))=f(0)$ , showing that  $a=0$ . Therefore  $f(a+f(0))=f(a)=f(0)$ , which shows that  $a+f(0)\in S$  as well.
In particular, we have  $f(2f(0))=f(3f(0))=f(0)$ . Now, by  $P(f(0),2f(0))$  we get  $f(3f(0))=2f(0)$  or  $f(2f(0))=3f(0)$ , both of which are contradictions.
Hence  $f(0)=0$ .</details>

<u>Prop 3.</u>  $-f$  is an involution.
We first show that if  $f(z)=0$  then  $z=0$ . To see this, notice that  $z+f(z)=z$  is a fixed point, and so  $z=0$ .
Now consider  $P(x,-f(x))$ . We know either  $x+f(-f(x))=f(0)=0$  or  $f(x+f(-f(x)))=0$ , both giving  $f(-f(x))=-x$ , or equivalently,  $-f(-f(x))=x$ , as desired.

<u>Prop 4.</u>  $f$  is *aquaesulian-Cauchy*: for every  $a,b\in \mathbb{Q}$ , either  $f(a)+f(b)=f(a+b)$  or  $f(-a)+f(a+b)=f(b)$ .
By  $P(x,-f(y))$  we see that either  $f(x-y)=f(x)-f(y)$  or  $f(f(x)-f(y))=x-y$ . Notice that for the latter, we get that $f(x)-f(y)=-f(-f(f(x)-f(y))))=-f(y-x)$ , or equivalently  $f(x)+f(y-x)=f(y)$ .
Now set  $y=a+b$  and  $x=b$  and we get the desired claim.

<u>Prop 5.</u> If  $f$  is aquaesulian-Cauchy, then for any  $x\in \mathbb{Q}$  and  $m\in \mathbb{Z}$  we have  $f(mx)+f(-mx)=f(x)+f(-x)$  or  $0$ .
<details><summary>Proof of Prop 5.</summary>This is probably the most involved part of the solution.
First, notice that if  $f(x)+f(-x)=0$  then there is nothing to prove as now we have  $f(x+b)=f(b)+f(x)$  whatsoever, showing that  $f(mx)=mf(x)$  and thus  $f(mx)+f(-mx) = 0$ .
Therefore, from now on, we assume that  $f(x)+f(-x)\neq 0$ . A consequence of this is that for any  $p,q\in \mathbb{Q}$  there exists a unique  $k_{p,q}\in \mathbb{Q}$  such that  $k_{p,q}f(x)-(p-k_{p,q}f(-x))=q$ .
For each  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , set  $A_n = k_{n,f(nx)}$  and  $B_n = k_{n,-f(-nx)}$ . We will show, by induction on  $n$ , that  $A_n, B_n$  are non-negative integers such that  $A_n-B_n = 0\textup{ or }1$ .
The base case  $n=1$  is trivial as  $A_1=1$  and  $B_1=0$ . Now suppose that the claim holds for  $n-1$  where  $n\geq 2$ .
First, notice, by aquaesulian-Cauchy-ness of  $f$ , that  $f(nx) = f((n-1)x)+f(x)$  or  $f(nx)=f((n-1)x)-f(-x)$ . This shows that  $A_n=A_{n-1}+1$  or  $A_n=A_{n-1}$ .
We also have  $-f(-nx)=-f(-(n-1)x)-f(-x)$  or  $-f(-nx)=f((n-1)x)-f(-x)$ , so  $B_n=B_{n-1}$  or  $A_{n-1}$ .
Hence  $A_n\geq A_{n-1}\geq B_n$ . It remains to show that  $A_n-B_n\leq 1$ .
To show this, for every  $m\in \mathbb{Z}$  set  $k(m) = k_{n,f((m+n)x)-f(mx)}$ , where in particular  $k(-n)=B_n$  and  $k(0)=A_n$ .
Notice that  $f((m+n+1)x)-f((m+n)x)$  is either  $f(x)$  or  $-f(-x)$ , and similarly  $f((m+1)x)-f(mx)$  is either  $f(x)$  or  $-f(-x)$  as well.
Therefore  $|k(m+1)-k(m)|\leq 1$  for all  $m\in \mathbb{Z}$ . However, by aquaesulian-Cauchy again, we must have  $f((m+n)x)-f(mx)$  is either  $f(nx)$  or  $-f(-nx)$ . Thus  $k(m)=A_n$  or  $B_n$ . By increasing  $m$  one-by-one from  $-n$  to  $0$ , we see that  $|A_n-B_n|\leq 1$ , so  $A_n-B_n\leq 1$ , as desired. Thus the induction is complete.

Finally, we know that  $f(mx)+f(-mx) = (A_m-B_m)(f(x)+f(-x))$  for all  $m\in\mathbb{N}$ . To extend to  $\mathbb{Z}$ , simply note that  $f(-mx)+f(mx) = f(mx)+f(-mx)$  and  $f(0)+f(0)=0$ .</details>

To wrap up, it suffices to show that if  $f(x)+f(-x), f(y)+f(-y)\neq 0$ , then  $f(x)+f(-x)=f(y)+f(-y)$ .
This is now simple as we can find their common divisor  $d$ , and then by Prop 5., we know if  $x=m_1d$  and  $y=m_2d$ , then  $f(x)+f(-x) = f(m_1d)+f(-m_1d) = f(d)+f(-d) = f(m_2d)+f(-m_2d)=f(y)+f(-y)$ .

Clearly  $f(r)+f(-r)=0$  if  $r$  is an integer, and it is equal to  $-2$  otherwise. It suffices to prove that this function is aquaesulian. <details><summary>Remark on additional solutions to this FE</summary>One additional solution to this FE is: 

Let  $P$  be a (possibly empty, finite, or infinite) set of primes. Now let  $Q$  be the set of all primes not in  $P$ . 

Choose  $S$  to be the union of  $0$  and all rational numbers such that the denominator (in simplest form) is not divisible by any prime in  $Q$ . Choose  $T$  to be the union of  $0$  and all rational numbers in  $(0,1)$  such that the denominator is not divisible by any prime in  $P$ . 

It's clear that  $S$  and  $T$  satisfy the first two conditions. Now we prove the third condition. 

If  $a + b = c + d = r$  and  $a,  c \in S, b, d \in T$  but  $a \ne c$ , then two different elements of  $T$  differ by an element in  $S$ . However, the denominator of this difference can't be divisible by any prime in  $P$ , meaning it must be  $1$  (since the difference is in  $S$ ). However, no two elements in  $T$  can differ by an integer since  $T \in [0,1)$ . Hence the uniqueness of the third condition is true. 

Now we show existence. Let  $\prod P$  and  $\prod Q$  be the product of all prime powers dividing  $P$  in the denominator  $r$  and product of all prime powers dividing  $Q$  in the denominator  $r$ , respectively. Now let  $m$  be the numerator of  $r$ . So  $r = \frac{m}{\prod P \prod Q}$ . Now choose integers  $a,b$  with  $a \prod Q + b \prod B = m$ , which is possible since  $\gcd(\prod P, \prod Q) = 1$ . Then note that  $\frac{a}{\prod P} + \frac{b}{\prod Q} = \frac{m}{ \prod P \prod Q} = r$ . Now we simply add  $b$  by enough multiples of  $ \prod Q$  (say  $k \prod Q$ ), so that  $0 \le b < \prod Q$ , and subtract  $a$  by  $k \prod P$ . We have that  $\frac{a - k \prod P}{\prod P} + \frac{b + k \prod Q}{\prod Q} = r$ ,  $\frac{a - k \prod P}{\prod P} \in S$ , and  $\frac{b + k \prod Q}{\prod Q} \in T$ , as desired.

Next, let  $g(x)=f(x)+f(-x)$ . We first note that  $g(a)\neq g(b)\implies f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$ . Assume not, then  $f(a+b) = -f(-a)+f(b) = f(a)-f(-b)$ , which implies  $g(a)=g(b)$ . By a similar logic,  $g(a)\neq g(b) \implies f(\pm a\pm b)=f(\pm a)+f(\pm b)$ , where there are  $4$  possible sign combinations, and so we deduce that for all  $a,b$ ,  $$ g(a)\neq g(b)\implies g(a+b) = g(a-b) = g(a)+g(b)\quad (\spadesuit). $$  We now assume for contradiction that for some  $a,b$ , we have  $g(a)\neq g(b)$  and neither are  $0$ . By  $(\spadesuit)$ , we have  $g(a+b) = g(a)+g(b)\neq g(a)$ , so using  $(\spadesuit)$  again, we get that  $g(b) = g(a+b)+g(a)$ , forcing  $g(a)=0$ , a contradiction.

<details><summary>Some ground work.</summary>We first show that  $f(0)=0$  and  $f(-f(x))=-x$ , in particular  $f$  is injective. The first part has two steps: show that  $0$  is a value of  $f$  and  $f(v)=0$  implies  $v=0$ . 

Substituting  $x=y=0$  gives  $f(f(0))=f(0)$ , i.e. if  $f(0)=u$  then  $f(u)=u$ . Substituting  $x=u, y=-f(u)$  into (*) gives  $x + f(y) = u+f(-u)$  and  $f(x) + y = f(u) - f(u) = 0$ , so either  $f(u + f(-u)) = 0$  or  $u = f(0) = u + f(-u)$ , i.e.  $f(-u) = 0$ . In either case, 0 is indeed a value of  $f$ , attained either by  $f(u + -f(u))$  or  $f(-u)$ . 

Now if  $f(v)=0$ , substituting  $x=y=v$  into (*) gives  $f(v)+v=0+v=v$ , so  $0=f(v)=v$ , as claimed. This thus gives  $f$  maps nonzero number to nonzero number and 0 to 0 (call this "condition A"). Finally, substituting  $y = -f(x)$  gives  $f(x)+y = 0$  and  $f(y)+x = f(-f(x))+x$ . By "condition A" and (*), we have  $f(-f(x))+x=0$ , so  $f(-f(x))=-x$ , as claimed.</details>

<details><summary>Some property exploitation.</summary>Denote, now,  $L = \{x: f(x)=x\}$  (i.e. the set of fixed points). We show / note the following property: 

- (1) From previous lemma: 0 is in  $L$ . 

- (2)  $L$  is closed under addition: indeed if  $x, y\in L$  then (*) implies  $f(x+y)=x+y$ . 

- (3)  $L$  is closed under negation: given  $f(-f(x))=-x$ , if  $x\in L$  then  $f(-x)=-x$ . 

- (4)  $L$  contains the set  $M = \{x + f(x): x\in\mathbb{Q}\}$ . 

- (5) If  $x + f(y)$  is in  $L$  then  $f(x) - f(y) = x - y$ . Indeed, by injectivity of  $f$ , if  $f(z) = x + f(y)$  then  $z = f(x) + y$ . Now (*) readily implies that  $f(x) + y = f(y) + x$ , so rearranging yields the conclusion. 

- (6) If  $x - y\in L$  then  $x + f(y)\in L$ . Indeed this follows from (4) that  $y + f(y)$  and  $x - y$  are both in  $L$ . 

- (7) If  $x\in L$ , then  $f(x + y) = x + f(y)$ . Indeed, due to (4) and (2) we have  $f(x + y + f(y)) = x + y + f(y)$  and (5) implies that (by substituting  $x + y$  into  $x$   $f(x + y) - f(y) = x$ , as claimed.</details>

<details><summary>Proving the bound (honestly, took some creativity).</summary>We may now show that  $c\le 2$ . To this end, note that  $r = 0$  means  $f(r) + f(-r)= 0$ , so it suffices to show that for each pair of rationals  $r_1, r_2$ , either  $f(r_1) + f(-r_1) = f(r_2) + f(-r_2)$ , or one of them is zero. 

Consider (*) again, but write  $x + f(y) = y + f(y) + x - y$ . The first condition (if true) and (7) means  $f(x)+y = f(x+f(y)) = f(y+f(y)+x-y) = y + f(y) + f(x - y)$ , i.e.  $f(x) = f(y) + f(x - y)$ . Similarly the second condition means  $f(y) = f(x) + f(y - x)$ . Thus we now have either  $f(x) = f(y) + f(x - y)$  or  $f(y) = f(x) + f(y - x)$  must hold (denote this as condition B1). Note also that, given this,  $f(x-y)+f(y-x)=0$  if and only if we have both  $f(x) = f(y) + f(x - y)$  and  $f(y) = f(x) + f(y - x)$  (denote this as condition B2). 

Now back to the rationals  $r_1, r_2$  that we set. We consider the following cases: 

- Case C0:  $f(r_1-r_2)+f(r_2-r_1)=0$ . Then by condition B,  $f(r_1) = f(r_2) + f(r_1 - r_2)$  and  $f(r_2) = f(r_1) + f(r_2 - r_1)$  both hold, and also  $f(-r_1) = f(-r_2) + f(r_2 - r_1)$  and  $f(-r_2) = f(-r_1) + f(r_1 - r_2)$  both hold. Thus  $f(r_1)-f(r_2) = f(-r_2)-f(-r_1)$ , i.e.  $f(r_1)+f(-r_1)=f(r_2)+f(-r_2)$ . 

- Case C1:  $f(r_1-r_2)+f(r_2-r_1)\neq 0$ . By condition B again, exactly one of  $f(r_1) = f(r_2) + f(r_1 - r_2)$  and  $f(r_2) = f(r_1) + f(r_2 - r_1)$  holds. 

W.l.o.g. suppose now that  $f(r_1) = f(r_2) + f(r_1 - r_2)$  but  $f(r_2) \neq f(r_1) + f(r_2 - r_1)$ . By condition B1 applied on  $x = r_2-r_1$  and  $y = r_2$ , 
we have  $f(r_2-r_1) = f(r_2) + (-r_1)$ . By condition B2 on  $x = r_2-r_1$  and then  $y = -r_1$ , we have one the following: 
\[f(r_2)+f(-r_2)=0\qquad \text{or}\qquad f(-r_1) \neq f(r_2-r_1)+f(-r_2) \]
In the first subcase we are done. In the second subcase we apply condition B1 on  $x=-r_1, y=-r_2$  to get $f(-r_2)=f(r_1-r_2) + f(-r_1)$ . 
Thus together with  $f(r_1) = f(r_2) + f(r_1 - r_2)$  we have  $f(r_1)+f(-r_1)=f(r_2)+f(-r_2)$ , as claimed.</details>

<details><summary>Some motivation on how to construct.</summary>The example of  $c = 2$  is shown above too many times (and honestly I have glanced through some spoiler before solving it), so here's my thought process. 

The set of fixed points  $L$  really behaves like a set of lattice points, so my initial thought was to write  $L$  as all rationals where there exists a set  $Q$  of primes and a function  $g:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Z}$  such that  $x\in L$  if and only if the power of each prime  $q\in Q$  is at least  $g(q)$ . For construction, I thought, okay let's make things easier and set  $L$  as integers, so  $x + f(x)$  should be an integer and  $f(x)=x$  for all integers  $x$ . 

Also the easiest function to (try) constructing is piecewise continuous, so let's try something like  $f(x) = \lfloor x\rfloor - \{x\} + 2\cdot\boldsymbol{1}_{\{x\} > w}$  for some  $w$  ( $\boldsymbol{1}_{K}$  is 1 if  $K$  is true and 0 if  $K$  is false).

Solution:  $c=2$  works by taking  $f(x)=x-2\{x\}$ , verification are similar to above posts so I won't reapeat it here. We will show now that  $c\le 2$ .

*Start with something that kills off the "OR" condition*

Let  $x=y$ , then  $f(x+f(x))=x+f(x) \Rightarrow x+f(x)$  is a fixed point of  $f$ . $x=0:$  then  $f(f(y))=f(0)+y$  OR  $f(f(0)+y)=f(y)$ Replace  $y\rightarrow f(y)$ , then  $f(f(f(y)))=f(0)+f(y)$  OR  $f(f(0)+f(y))=f(f(y))$ . $y=-f(x):$  then  $f(x+f(-f(x))) = 0$  OR  $f(0) = x + f(-f(x))$ Suppose the first case holds for some  $x$ , then  $0$  is already in the kernel of  $f$ .
If the second case holds for all  $x$ , then take  $x=f(0) \Rightarrow f(-f(f(0)))=0$ .
This proves that  $0$  in  $Im(f)$ .
So there exist some  $k$  with  $f(k)=0$ . Then  $k+f(k)=k$  is a fixed point of  $f$ , so  $f(k)=k$ , but  $f(k)=0$ ! So  $k=0$ . 
This means  $k=0\iff f(k)=0$ , and  $f(0)=0$ .

So  $f(x+f(-f(x)))=0$  OR  $0=x+f(-f(x))$ . 
If the first case is true, then by injectivity at  $0$ , then  $x+f(-f(x))=0$ , which is the second case.
So the second case is always true, so  $f(-f(x))=-x$ . In particular  $f$  is bijective.

Now we manipulate the conditions from this result: $f(x+f(y)) = f(x) + y$  OR  $f(f(x)+y) = x + f(y)$ .  $y\rightarrow -f(y)$ , then  $f(x+f(-f(y)))=f(x)-f(y)$  OR  $f(f(x)-f(y))=x+f(-f(y))$ .  $$ \Rightarrow f(x-y)=f(x)-f(y) \quad \text{OR} \quad f(f(x)-f(y))=x-y $$  From the second condition, we get:  $f(-f(f(x)-f(y)))=f(y-x)$   $\Rightarrow f(y)-f(x)=f(y-x)$ .
So  $f(x-y)=f(x)-f(y)$  OR  $f(y-x)=f(y)-f(x)$  for all  $x$ ,  $y$ .

*Now we try to tackle the problem, but we need a way to keep track which conditions are true. Best visualization will be a graph where the vertices are the values for  $x$  and  $y$ .* 

Denote  $P(x\rightarrow y)$  OR  $P(y \rightarrow x)$  to mean:  $f(x+f(y)) = f(x) + y$  [which we write  $P(x\rightarrow y)$ ] OR  $f(f(x)+y) = x + f(y)$  [which we write  $P(y\rightarrow x)$ ]. 
So the condition is that for all  $x$ ,  $y$ , then  $P(x\rightarrow y)$  OR  $P(y\rightarrow x)$ .
In particular,  $P(x\rightarrow x)$  is always true.

*Substitute something that forces  $f(r)+f(-r)$  to appear*

Take any real  $r$ , replace  $x$  by  $x+f(-r)$  and  $y$  by  $r$ :   $$ \Rightarrow f(x+f(-r)+f(r))=f(x+f(-r))+r \quad \text{OR} \quad f(f(x+f(-r))+r)=x+f(-r)+f(r) \quad (*) $$   

*Let's do some wishful thinking: Let's suppose  $f(x+f(-r))=-r+f(x)$  so to simplify the second case above (of course there is the other case, but we can think about it later)*

If  $P(x\rightarrow -r)$ , then  $f(x+f(-r))=-r+f(x)$ .
Then the first condition in  $(*)$  becomes  $f(x+f(-r)+f(r))=f(x) \Rightarrow f(-r)+f(r)=0$ .
While the second condition becomes  $f(f(x))=x+f(-r)+f(r) \Rightarrow f(r)+f(-r)=f(f(x))-x$ .

So, if  $P(x\rightarrow -r)$ , then  $f(r)+f(-r)=0$  OR  $f(f(x))-x$ .
Likewise if  $P(x\rightarrow r)$ , then  $f(r)+f(-r)=0$  OR  $f(f(x))-x$ .

*This is a very strong restriction on the possible values of  $f(r)+f(-r)$ ! Now we can compare two different values of  $r$ .*

Suppose now we have two reals  $u$  and  $v$  where  $f(u)+f(-u)\neq 0$ , and  $f(v)+f(-v)\neq 0$ , 
Then WLOG  $P(u\rightarrow v)$  is true, then  $f(v)+f(-v)=f(f(u))-u$ .
But  $P(u\rightarrow u)$  is always true, so  $f(u)+f(-u)=f(f(u))-u$  !!

So  $f(u)+f(-u)=f(v)+f(-v)$  for any reals  $u$  and  $v$ , if both  $f(u)+f(-u)$  and  $f(v)+f(-v)$  are non-zero.
So  $c\le 2$ .

QED

Here is my solution. Please check for any errors.   \section*{Solution} 
We aim to show that \( c = 2 \) is the smallest possible value. To achieve this, we approach the problem using a novel framework involving graph theory and symmetry.

\subsection*{Step 1: Key Transformation and Symmetry} 
Define:
\[
T(r) = f(r) + f(-r), \quad \text{where } r \in \mathbb{Q}.
\]
The goal is to determine how \( T(r) \) behaves under the constraints given by the functional equations.

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Annotation:} \textit{The transformation } T(r) \textit{ simplifies the functional equation by focusing on the symmetry between } r \textit{ and } -r. \textit{ This reduction allows us to analyze } f(r) \textit{ indirectly.}}
\]

\subsection*{Step 2: Functional Implications of Symmetry} 
\textbf{Case Analysis for the Functional Equations}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item From \( f(x + f(y)) = f(x) + y \), setting \( x = 0 \) gives:
    \[
    f(f(y)) = y + f(0).
    \]
    Thus, \( f \) is surjective, and \( f(0) \) plays a central role.
    \item From \( f(f(x) + y) = x + f(y) \), setting \( y = 0 \) gives:
    \[
    f(f(x)) = x + f(0).
    \]
    Combining these, we deduce:
    \[
    f(f(x)) = x + f(0) \quad \text{and} \quad f(f(0)) = 0.
    \]
\end{enumerate}

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Annotation:} \textit{These equations reveal that } f(f(x)) \textit{ has a highly structured form, allowing us to infer further properties about } T(r).}
\]

\subsection*{Step 3: Graph-Theoretic Model} 
We interpret \( f \) as defining a directed graph \( G \) over the set \( \mathbb{Q} \), where an edge \( x \to y \) exists if:
\[
f(x + f(y)) = f(x) + y.
\]
This graph-theoretic interpretation reveals:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The functional equations correspond to symmetries in \( G \), forming "cycles" due to the injective and surjective nature of \( f \).
    \item The transformation \( T(r) = f(r) + f(-r) \) corresponds to analyzing the structure of these cycles.
\end{enumerate}

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Annotation:} \textit{The graph-based approach transforms the problem into one of studying symmetry and boundedness in a graph, an innovative perspective.}}
\]

\subsection*{Step 4: Bounding \( T(r) \)} 
By symmetry, \( T(r) \) is invariant under \( r \to -r \), i.e., \( T(r) = T(-r) \). Consider:
\[
T(r) = f(r) + f(-r).
\]

\textbf{Key Observation:}
- For any \( r \), \( T(r) \) must take at most two values:
\[
T(r) = f(0) \quad \text{or} \quad T(r) = 0.
\]

\textbf{Why?}
\begin{itemize}
    \item If \( f(r) = r + c \) (a linear solution), then:
    \[
    T(r) = f(r) + f(-r) = (r + c) + (-r + c) = 2c.
    \]
    \item If \( f(r) \neq r + c \), the symmetry forces \( T(r) \) to collapse to a single additional value (e.g., \( 0 \)).
\end{itemize}

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Annotation:} \textit{This step finalizes the bound on } T(r), \textit{ ensuring that at most two distinct values are possible regardless of } f.}
\]

\subsection*{Step 5: Conclusion} 
Thus, the smallest possible value of \( c \) is:
\[
\boxed{2}.
\]
This bound holds universally across all aquaesulian functions \( f \).

solutionThe answer is $c=2$ .**Claim:** $f$ is injective. Notice that $x+f(x)$ is a fixed point of $f$ for all $x$ . If there were $a\neq b$ such that $f(a)=f(b)$ , then suppose wlog that $f(a+f(b))=f(a)+b$ (otherwise swap $a$ and $b$ ). We get \[f(a)+b=f(a+f(b))=f(a+f(a))=a+f(a)\] Which implies $a=b$ , a contradiction. $\blacksquare$ It's easy now to see that $f(0)=0$ . Plugging $x\mapsto -y+f(-y)$ (which is a fixed point) yields \[f(-y+f(-y)+f(y))=f(-y) \quad \text{or} \quad f(f(-y))=-y+f(-y)+f(y)\] In particular, if $f(y)+f(-y)\neq 0$ we have $f(f(-y))+y=f(-y)+f(y)$ Suppose now we have $x\neq y$ such that $f(x)+f(-x)$ and $f(y)+f(-y)$ both aren't $0$ and assume wlog that $f(x+f(y))=f(x)+y$ . Plugging $x\mapsto x+f(y)$ , $y\mapsto z$ yields \[f(x+f(y)+f(z))=f(x)+y+z \quad \text{or} \quad f(f(x)+y+z)=x+f(y)+f(z)\] In particular, replacing $z$ with $-y$ will give us \[f(x+f(y)+f(-y))=f(x) \quad \text{or} \quad f(f(x))=x+f(y)+f(-y)\] The first case can't happen since injectivity gives $f(y)+f(-y)=0$ so \[f(y)+f(-y)=f(f(x))-x=f(x)+f(-x)\] Therefore, $f(x)+f(-x)$ can only attain a maximum of $2$ values. For the construction, pick $f=\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor -\{x\}$ . Since for all $x\not\in \mathbb Z$ $\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor -x\right\rfloor =-1$ and $\{x\}+\{-x\}=1$ we have that $f(x)+f(-x)\in\{0,-2\}$ . Also, if $\{x\}\ge\{y\}$ a quick calculation yields \[f(x+f(y))=f(x)+y\] and so $f$ is aquaesulian. $\blacksquare$ **Remarks:** For the record, I don't think this is that hard. There are lots of things you can prove that I didn't end up using in the solution. I think the main idea was to try $x\mapsto x+f(y)$ in the FE and see what that can give you. After a bit of trial and error, this actually finishes the problem! Overall a beautiful FE and I'm happy that this appeared on the IMO.

We claim the the answer is  $c=2$ . We first show that there are at most  $2$  rational numbers of the form  $f(x)+f(-x)$  for any aquaesulian  $f$ . Let  $P(x,y)$  be the given statement.**Claim:  $f(x)=0\iff x=0$****Proof:**
We first show  $f(0)=0$ . From  $P(x,x)$  we have \[f(f(x)+x)=f(x)+x\] Taking  $x=0$  we have \[f(f(0))=f(0)\] and taking  $x=f(0)$  we have \[f(2f(0))=2f(0)\] Taking  $P(0,f(0))$  we have \[[f(0)=2f(0)\quad\vee\quad 2f(0)=f(0)]\implies f(0)=0\] Now suppose FTSOC we have  $f(x)=0$  for some  $x\neq 0$ . Then for all  $y$ , from  $P(x,y)$  we have \[[f(x+f(y))=y\quad\vee\quad f(y)=x+f(y)]\implies f(x+f(y))=y\] Then  $f$  is surjective, and taking  $y$  with  $f(y)=-x$ , we have \[y=f(x+f(y))=0\] and thus  $x=0$ . This is a contradiction, and so there is no such  $x$ .**Claim:  $f$  is injective****Proof:**
From  $P(x,-f(x))$ , we get \[[f(x+f(-f(x)))=0\quad\vee\quad 0=x+f(-f(x))]\implies f(-f(x))=-x\] Then from  $P(x,-f(y))$ , we get \[f(x-y)=f(x)-f(y)\quad\vee\quad f(f(x)-f(y))=x-y\] Denote this statement by  $Q(x,y)$ . If we ever have  $f(x)=f(y)$ , then from  $Q(x,y)$  we have \[[f(x-y)=0\quad\vee\quad 0=x-y]\implies x=y\] So,  $f$  is injective.**Claim:  $f$  is surjective****Proof:**
From  $Q(x+y,y)$ , we get \[f(x)=f(x+y)-f(y)\quad\vee\quad f(f(x+y)-f(y))=x\] Taking  $y=f(x)$ , we get \[[f(f(x))=x\quad\vee\quad f(x+f(x)-f(f(x)))=x]\implies f(x+f(x)-f(f(x)))=x\] Then  $f$  is surjective. Also, \[f(x)-f^{-1}(x)=f(f(x))-x\]**Claim:  $f(f(x))-x$  takes on at most  $2$  values****Proof:**
We have that  $Q(x+y,y)$  implies \[f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\quad\vee\quad f(x+y)=f^{-1}(x)+f(y)\] Now, for any  $x,y$  we have  $f(x+f(y))=f(x)+y$  or  $f(f(x)+y)=x+f(y)$ . The former yields
\begin{align*}
    &f(x+f(y))=f(x)+y
    \implies&f(x)+f(f(y))=f(x)+y\quad\vee\quad f^{-1}(x)+f(f(y))=f(x)+y
    \implies&f(f(y))=y\quad\vee\quad f(x)-f^{-1}(x)=f(f(y))-y
    \implies&f(f(y))=y\quad\vee\quad f(f(x))-x=f(f(y))-y
\end{align*}
Performing a similar argument for the latter, we get \[f(f(x))=x\quad\vee\quad f(f(y))=y\quad\vee\quad f(f(x))-x=f(f(y))-y\] It follows that there is some nonzero constant  $r$  such that \[f(f(x))-x=0\quad\vee\quad f(f(x))-x=r\] for all  $x$ .**Claim:  $f(x)+f(-x)$  takes on at most  $2$  values****Proof:**
We have \[f(f(-f(x)))=f(-x)\implies [f(x)+f(-x)=0\quad\vee\quad f(x)+f(-x)=r]\] as desired.**We now have that  $c=2$  is a suitable upper bound.** We now further characterize  $f$  achieving  $c=2$ . Let  $A$  be the set of  $x$  for which  $f(f(x))=x$  and  $B$  be the set of  $x$  for which  $f(f(x))=x+r$ . We need  $B$  to be nonempty.**Claim:  $A$  is an additive subgroup of  $\mathbb Q$****Proof:**
It is clear that  $A$  is closed under  $f$  and  $f^{-1}$ . We need to show that  $A$  is a subgroup of  $\mathbb Q$ . We already have  $0\in A$ . Note that if  $x\in A$ , then \[[f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\quad\vee\quad f(x+y)=f^{-1}(x)+f(y)]\implies f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\] Performing a similar argument for  $y$ , we have \[[x\in A\quad\vee\quad y\in A]\implies f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\] Now consider any  $x,y\in A$ . Then \[f(f(x+y))=f(f(x)+f(y))=f(f(x))+f(f(y))=x+y\] and  $x+y\in A$ . Also, if  $x\in A$ , then \[f(f(-x))=f(f(-f(f(x))))=f(-f(x))=-x\] and  $-x\in A$ . Then indeed  $A$  is an additive subgroup of  $\mathbb Q$ .**Claim:  $f(x)=x$  for all  $x\in A$****Proof:**
We already have that  $f$  is additive over  $A$ . Consider any nonzero  $x,y\in A$ . Picking nonzero integers  $m,n$  such that  $mx=ny$ , we have \[mf(x)=f(mx)=f(ny)=nf(y)\implies \frac{f(x)}{x}=\frac{f(y)}{y}\] Then  $\frac{f(x)}{x}$  is constant over nonzero  $x\in A$ . Now, for any  $x\in B$ , we have that  $f(x)+x$  and  $f(f(x))+f(x)=f(x)+x+r$  are both fixed points of  $f$ . At least one of these is nonzero; then since any fixed point is obviously in  $A$ , we have that  $A$  contains a nonzero fixed point. Then the constant value of  $\frac{f(x)}{x}$  over nonzero  $x\in A$  is  $1$  and we have \[x\in A\implies f(x)=x\]**Claim:  $r\mathbb Z\subset A$****Proof:**
We will show that for any  $x\in B$  we have  $x-r\in B$ . Now, since  $A$  is closed under  $f$  and  $f^{-1}$ ,  $B$  must be as well. Now, for any  $x\in B$ , we have  $f^{-1}(f^{-1}(x))\in B$  and \[x\in B\implies f^{-1}(f^{-1}(x))=f(f(f^{-1}(f^{-1}(x))))-r=x-r\] Then  $f^{-1}(f^{-1}(x))=x-r$  is in  $B$ , as desired. Now, since  $0\in A$ , this implies  $r\in A$ . It follows that  $r\mathbb Z\subseteq A$ . Now suppose FTSOC  $A=r\mathbb Z$ . Since  $f(x)+x\in A$  we have that \[f(x)\equiv -x\pmod A\] We also remark that we have \[y\in A\implies f(x+y)=f(x)+y\] Then there is a natural interpretation of  $f$  as function from  $\mathbb Q / A$  to itself. Now suppose FTSOC there is  $x\in B$  with  $f(x)\equiv x\pmod A$ . This would yield  $f(x)=x+kr$  for some  $k\in\mathbb Z$ . Then \[f(x)=f^{2k}(x)\implies f^{4k-2}(x)=x\implies x+(2k-1)r=x\] which is a contradiction. However, we now have \[f\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)\equiv -\frac{r}{2}\equiv \frac{r}{2}\pmod A\] which is a contradiction. Then indeed  $A\neq r\mathbb Z$ .**We now construct aquaesulian  $f$  achieving  $c=2$ .** Let  $A$  be the set of  $x$  such that  $\nu_2(x)\geq 0$ . It is easy to see that  $A$  is an additive subgroup of  $\mathbb Q$ . Let  $T$  be the set of rationals in  $[0,1)$  whose denominator in simplest form is a power of  $2$ . We show that each element of  $\mathbb Q/A$  is uniquely represented by an element of  $T$ . We first show that any rational is equivalent to an element of  $T$  modulo  $A$ . For any  $x$  such that  $\nu_p(x)<0$  for some  $p>2$ , we can add a number of the form  $\frac{a}{p^{\nu_p(x)}}$  where  $a\in\mathbb Z$  to  $x$  to increase  $\nu_p(x)$  by  $1$ . By repeating this process, we can show that  $x$  is equivalent to a rational whose denominator in simplest form is a power of  $2$ . Then by adding a suitable integer we have that  $x$  is equivalent to an element of  $T$ . We now show that each element of  $T$  is distinct modulo  $A$ . The difference of any distinct elements in  $T$  belongs to  $T\setminus\{0\}$ ; however, no element of  $T\setminus\{0\}$  is in  $A$ , as desired.

Then every  $x$  can be uniquely represented in the form  $\alpha+\lambda$  for some  $\alpha\in A,\lambda\in T$ ; then take  $f(x)$  such that \[f(\alpha+\lambda)=\alpha-\lambda\] We show that  $f$  is aquaesulian. We can check that  $f(x+y)=f(x)+y$  for all  $x$  whenever  $y\in A$ . It then suffices to check  $P(x,y)$  for whenever  $x,y\in T$ . Noting that  $f(0)=0$ , it is easy to check the cases of  $x=0$ ,  $y=0$ , and  $x=y$ , so assume WLOG  $0<x<y$ . Then  $y-x\in T$  and \[f(f(x)+y)=f(y-x)=x-y=x+f(y)\] In all cases,  $P(x,y)$  holds, and  $f$  is aquaesulian. Also, we have  $f(x)+f(-x)=0$  for  $x\in A$ , and for  $x\notin A$ , writing  $x=\alpha+\lambda$  we have \[f(x)+f(-x)=f(\alpha+\lambda)+f((-\alpha-1)+(1-\lambda))=(\alpha-\lambda)+((-\alpha-1)-(1-\lambda))=-2\] Then this  $f$  achieves  $c=2$ .</details>

\]
Our goal is to show \(P\) cannot be injective on the positive rationals, which forces it to be constant there.


Choose any \(a,b\) in the rationals with \(g(a)\neq g(b)\), and set
\[
u=a+f(-b),
\quad
v=b+f(-a).
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
g(u)&=u+f(u)

     =a+f(-b)+\bigl(f(a)-b\bigr)
     =g(a)-g(b),
g(v)&=v+f(v)
     =\bigl(b+f(-a)\bigr)+f\bigl(b+f(-a)\bigr)
     =b+f(-a)+\bigl(f(b)-a\bigr)
     =g(b)-g(a)
     =-\,\bigl(g(a)-g(b)\bigr).
\end{align*}
Set
\[

\quad
s=\frac{u-v}2,
\]
so that \(u=t+s\) and \(v=t-s\).  Hence
\[
g(t+s)=g(u),
\quad
g(t-s)=g(v)=-\,g(u),

\[
P(t+s)=g(t+s)+g(-(t+s)),

stem_md:
Turbo the snail plays a game on a board with  $2024$  rows and  $2023$  columns. There are hidden monsters in  $2022$  of the cells. Initially, Turbo does not know where any of the monsters are, but he knows that there is exactly one monster in each row except the first row and the last row, and that each column contains at most one monster.

Turbo makes a series of attempts to go from the first row to the last row. On each attempt, he chooses to start on any cell in the first row, then repeatedly moves to an adjacent cell sharing a common side. (He is allowed to return to a previously visited cell.) If he reaches a cell with a monster, his attempt ends and he is transported back to the first row to start a new attempt. The monsters do not move, and Turbo remembers whether or not each cell he has visited contains a monster. If he reaches any cell in the last row, his attempt ends and the game is over.

Determine the minimum value of  $n$  for which Turbo has a strategy that guarantees reaching the last row on the  $n$ -th attempt or earlier, regardless of the locations of the monsters.

*Proposed by Cheuk Hei Chu, Hong Kong*
solution_md: The answer is $\boxed{n=3}$ . ----- **Claim:** $n\geq 3$ . *Proof.* It is easy to see that $n=1$ does not guarantee victory: There may be a monster hiding in any cell in the second row, and if the first cell in the second row we move to has a monster, then the attempt is over. To see why $n=2$ does not guarantee victory, suppose we failed in our first attempt by falling victim to the monster at $(2, i)$ for some $i\in[1, 2023]$ . Hence, the second row except the cell $(2, i)$ is now safe. The safe $(3, i)$ cell is inaccessible from here, and any accessible cell in the third row may hide a monster in it. The first cell in the third row we move to could contain a monster, and that would end the attempt there. $\blacksquare$ ----- We proceed to show that $n=3$ is sufficient. Use the first attempt to scan the second row. **Case 1:** The monster in the second row is at $(2, 1)$ or $(2, 2023)$ . WLOG, say it is hiding in the cell $(2, 1)$ . In our second attempt, we go along the path $$ (1,2)\to(2,2)\to(2,3)\to\text{P}\to(2024,2023) $$ where a 'staircase' path $\text{P}$ is defined by $$ (3,3)\to(3,4)\to(4,4)\to(4,5)\to\cdots\to(2022,2023)\to(2023,2023). $$ If path $\text{P}$ is safe, then we are done. We have a  $(n+2)\times (n+1)$  board with  $n=2022$  and  $n$  is even. We  $0$ -index rows but  $1$ -index columns. Each row, except the  $0$ -th and last rows, has a monster. For a square  $S$ , we use the notation:  $S+(i,j)$  to denote the square  $i$  rows below  $S$  and  $j$  columns to the right of  $S$ . We will prove that the answer is X, where <details><summary>Answer, value of X</summary>X=3</details>.

Before proceeding, I'd like to explain how an intuitive, heuristic, and logical way to arrive at the answer, since it seems like at first, it was highly surprising for a lot of us at first. It is not rigorous! But it's my attempt at <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>explaining why most reasonable attempts at proving a non-trivial lower bound probably won't work</details>. <details><summary>My intuition to arrive at X (not part of the solution)</summary>I think it is reasonable to, at first, expect  $X=n$  or  $\frac{n}{2}$  (perhaps cutting the board in half and using symmetry). Maybe using two symmetries it could be  ${X=2024}/{4}$ , or perhaps a more extravagant answer like  $X=O(\sqrt{n})$  or  $X=O(\log n)$ . In fact,  $\log_2(n)$  doesn't seem crazy. From an Information Theory perspective, we can think of each attempt as giving us a bit of information (either it worked or it didn't), and perhaps we need at least  $n$  bits of information to guarantee a safe path. However, our first realization is that each attempt gives us **a lot more** than one bit of data. Indeed, each path uses at least  $n$  squares, and there are  $\ge n$  possible results, because we also discover exactly where the monster is on that path.

The second clue is that Turbo can go backwards and revisit squares. Immediately we know this is either useless, or it must be a key part of our strategy. If it's useless, we should be able to prove that any strategy that works can be adapted to a strategy that also works but never goes backwards (this could even be a Lemma that gives 1/2 points if this were the solution). I spent some time trying to prove this and didn't get anywhere; this made me suspect going backwards must actually be used in the solution. In fact, without going backwards, you always have at most  $3$  new squares to visit. But with going backwards, you in fact have  $P$  new squares you can visit, where  $P$  is the "perimeter" of the region of squares you have currently visited (i.e. the set of squares you haven't visited but are adjacent to one you have). The extra flexibility makes the number of different possible paths to victory VERY large, roughly  $O((n^2)^n)$ , because "most of the time"  $P\approx O(n)$ .

Now, each strategy can be thought of as a directed tree of depth  $X$  with an extra terminal "winning" node. Each node is a path (an attempt at winning). If a node's path visits  $s$  squares, then it has  $s+1$  children: either we won and the edge arrives at the winning node, or we fail and we get  $s$  new nodes depending on which square the monster was on. Thus, each node has at least  $O(n)$  children but can have as many as  $O(n^2)$  children if we start going backwards. Thus, the number of nodes is between  $O(n^{X-1})$  and  $O(n^{2(X-1)})$ .

Thus, even for small  $X$ , we get an absurd number of nodes. Specially compared to the number of possible configurations of monsters: there are roughly  $(n+1)!$ . In fact, the number of possible configurations should greatly exceed the number of nodes for an optimal tree: almost any given serious "candidate path" will work for many different configurations, e.g. just using one column works for  $n!$  configurations. Thus we'd only need roughly  $\frac{(n+1)!}{n!}=n+1$  nodes, not  $n^n$  or even  $n^{\log n}$ .

All of this hints at  $X=O(1)$ .</details>

<details><summary>Proof that X tries suffice</summary>Consider the pyramid  $P$  comprised of the middle  $n-1$  squares of the first row, the middle  $n-3$  squares of the second row, and so on, until we have the middle square of the  $\frac{n}{2}$ -th row. On our first try, we can (try to) traverse  $P$ ; the exact order won't matter as long as we go row-by-row.**Case 1**: We die before completing  $P$ .
Assume we die on the  $i$ -th row,  $1\le i\le \frac{n}{2}$ , on square  $S$ . If we reach the square below  $S$ , i.e.  $S+(1,0)$ , we win, because that column only has one monster (on  $S$ ), so we can use it to safely descend. (The remainder of the proof for this case will assume, for linguistic convenience, that  $i>1$ , but the case  $i=1$  is identical). Now, by construction, we can reach  $S+(-1,-1), S+(-1,0), S+(-1,1)$  safely using  $P$ . Next, we can attempt to go around  $S$  to the right  $S+(-1,1) \to S+(0,1) \to S(1,1) \to S+(1,0)$  or similarly the left. At most one of these attempts will fail, since only one of  $S(1,1)$  and  $S(1,-1)$  can have a monster in it. Thus, using 2 more tries, we can win.**Case 2**: We complete  $P$ .
We're now at the middle square of row  $\frac{n}{2}$  having died zero times; call this square  $M$ . Walk the entirety of this row until we find a monster and die. WLOG it is on square  $S$  to the **left** of  $M$ . On our second try, we traverse  $P$  again to reach  $M$ . Now, consider the following staircase  $Q$ : starting at  $M$ , draw the diagonal going right-and-down, and the horizontal line going right; these define an angle of  $45^\circ$ , which along with the right edge of the board defines the limits of  $Q$ . It has  $\frac{n}{2}+1$  squares on the row of  $M$ ,  $\frac{n}{2}$  squares on the next row, and so on, and it has  $0$  squares on the last (monster-free) row.

We now (try to) traverse  $Q$  row-by-row. We won't die on the first row of  $Q$  because the monster on that row is to the left of  $M$ . If we succeed in traversing  $Q$ , when we reach its last square, we've won. Otherwise, we die at some point. Assume we die on  $T = M + (i, j)$ , where  $j\ge i \ge 1$ . Then, on our third try:

1. Traverse  $P$  to reach  $M$ 2. Traverse  $Q$  until you reach  $T+(-1, -1)$ .
3. You can now safely walk  $T +(-1,-1) \to T+(0,-1) \to T+(0,-2) \to \ldots \to T+(0,-k)$ , where  $k$  is such that  $T+(0,-k)$  is on the same column as  $S$ . This is because  $T$  has a monster, so the rest of its row is vacant.
4. Since  $S$  has a monster and is above  $T+(0,-k)$ , the rest of that column is vacant. Thus, we can safely traverse  $T+(0,-k) \to T+(1,-k) \to \ldots \to T+(\ell, -k)$  such that the last square is on the last row.

We've won!</details>

<details><summary>Proof that X-1 tries do not suffice</summary>We prove  $2$  tries can never guarantee a win. We can always die on our very first step into the first row, say on square  $S$ . Then, on our second try, when we attempt to step into the second row, we cannot go directly into  $S+(1,0)$ , since that square is only accessible from above using  $S$ , but  $S$  has a monster. Thus, we must use a square on the second row that is on a different column from  $S$ . That square can also always contain a monster! Thus,  $2$  tries can never suffice.</details>

If you encounter another monster while rerouting, restart at that column and reroute around the new monster. Repeat until you bypass the connected blob of monsters. 

A worst-case monster arrangement for this strategy is a diagonal line stretching from the end of column  $1$  to the start of column  $2022$ , with column  $2023$  free. This would also require  $2023$  attempts.

Can we do better? Yes, and here’s how:

The simple algorithm requires  $n$  steps to find any possible path through  $n$  columns but fails because the first  $2022$  attempts are tested on impossible column configurations. Note that every impossible configuration consists of monsters arranged in a diagonal line.

To improve, consider the following algorithm:  
First, check the first and last columns. If neither column is the gap, observe that there cannot be a diagonal line stretching from the monster in column  $1$  to the monster in column  $2023$ . This guarantees a possible path through the  $2023$  columns. Next, test the middle column. One or both sides of the split cannot form a solid diagonal line, so at least one half contains a valid path. Repeat this process, testing the middle of the remaining side, until the gap is found.

Since the number of columns is  $n = 2023$ , the number of steps required is approximately:
\[
2 \text{ (initial setup)} + \log_2(n) \text{ (halvings)} + 1 \text{ (final check)}.
\]
For  $n = 2023$ ,  $\log_2(2023) \approx 11$ , so the total number of steps is:
\[
2 + 11 + 1 = 14.
\]

This binary search-like algorithm reduces the number of attempts from  $2023$  to  $14$ , providing a significant improvement.

A sleeping rabbit lies in the interior of a convex  $2024$ -gon. A hunter picks three vertices of the polygon and he lays a trap which covers the interior and the boundary of the triangular region determined by them. Determine the minimum number of times he needs to do this to guarantee that the rabbit will be trapped.

*Proposed by Anant Mudgal and Rohan Goyal*
solution_md:
It isn't as easy as the people above have said, I would say it's a nice problem.

First, observe that each interior angle must be entirely covered, and each triangle contributes  $180^{\circ}$ , while the sum of all the interior angles is  $180\cdot 2022^{\circ}$ , hence we must have to make at least  $2022$  triangles. Consider a triangulation of the polygon, which clearly works, hence our answer is  $\boxed{2022}$ .

Let  $x_1, x_2 \dots, x_{2024}$  be non-negative real numbers such that  $x_1 \le  x_2\cdots \le x_{2024}$ , and  $x_1^3 + x_2^3 + \dots + x_{2024}^3 = 2024$ . Prove that

\[\sum_{1 \le i < j \le 2024} (-1)^{i+j} x_i^2 x_j \ge -1012.\]

*Proposed by Shantanu Nene*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution 1</summary>We want that
    \[\sum_{1 \le i < j \le 2024} (-1)^{i+j} x_i^2 x_j \ge -1012.\]Now, observe that the LHS is \[-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{1012}x_{2i-1}^2x_{2i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{1012}\left(\left(x_{2i}^2-x_{2i-1}^2\right)\left(\sum_{i<j\le 1012}(x_{2j}-x_{2j-1})\right)\right).\]But,  $x_{2i}^2\ge x_{2i-1}^2$  and  $x_{2j}\ge x_{2j-1}$ , thus we will be done if  $\sum\limits_{i=1}^{1012}x_{2i-1}^2x_{2i}\le 1012$ . But, \[3x_{2i-1}^2x_{2i}\le 2x_{2i-1}^3+x_{2i}^3 \le 3\cdot \frac{x_{2i-1}^3+x_{2i}^3}{2}.\]Thus, we just need  $\sum\limits_{i=1}^{1012} \frac{x_{2i-1}^3+x_{2i}^3}2 \le 1012$  but this is precisely the given condition so we are done!

Observe that all equalities hold if  $x_{2i-1}=x_{2i}$  for all  $i$ .  $\blacksquare$</details>

<details><summary>Solution 2</summary>We use induction on  $k$  to show the following: given non-negative reals  $x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\le x_{2k}$ , we have   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{2k}x_i^3+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le 2k}(-1)^{i+j}x_i^2x_j\ge 0 $$  with equality iff  $x_{2i-1}=x_{2i}$ . This suffices since  $x_1^3 + x_2^3 + \dots + x_{2024}^3 = 2024$ .

Note that the left-hand side can be written as  $x_{2k}^3-2cx_{2k}+d$ , where   $$ c=x_{2k-1}^2-x_{2k-2}^2+\cdots-x_2^2+x_1^2 $$   and   $$ d=\sum_{i=1}^{2k-1}x_i^3+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le 2k-1}(-1)^{i+j}x_i^2x_j\ge 0 $$  are independent of  $x_{2k}$ . Consider the function  $f(x)=x^3-2cx+d$ . Its derivative is  $3x^2-2c$ , and so  $f$  is increasing as long as  $x^2\ge 2c/3$ . However,   $$ c=x_{2k-1}^2+(-x_{2k-2}^2+x_{2k-3}^2)+\cdots+(-x_2^2+x_1^2)\le x_{2k-1}^2, $$  so either  $c<0$ , in which case  $x_{2k-1}^2\ge 0 >2c/3$ , or  $c\ge 0$ , in which case  $x_{2k-1}^2\ge c\ge 2c/3$ .

Thus we must have   $$ f(x_{2k})\ge f(x_{2k-1})=\sum_{i=1}^{2k-2}x_i^3+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le 2k-2}(-1)^{i+j}x_i^2x_j $$  and the rest follows by induction.  $\blacksquare$</details>
